gloss: gō (≈180 ml; traditional volume unit, esp. for rice and sake)

definitions.gloss: gō; traditional unit of volume (≈180 ml)
definitions.explanation: A traditional Japanese unit of volume, approximately 180 milliliters. Most commonly used for measuring uncooked rice when cooking and for serving sake. Ten {合|ごう} make one {升|しょう}.

definitions.gloss: tenth of the way up a mountain (counter for mountain-climbing stages)
definitions.explanation: A counter dividing a mountain's height into ten stages from base to summit. Famously used for Mt. Fuji, where stations are labeled {一合目|いちごうめ} through {十合目|じゅうごうめ} (the summit).

examples.japanese: ⟦{米|こめ}→米：01323_kome⟧⟦を→を：00422_wo⟧{二合|にごう}⟦{炊|た}いた→炊く：02127_taku⟧。
examples.english: I cooked two gō of rice.

examples.japanese: {今晩|こんばん}は⟦{日本酒|にほんしゅ}→日本酒：12954_nihonshu⟧⟦を→を：00422_wo⟧{一合|いちごう}⟦{飲|の}んだ→飲む：00322_nomu⟧。
examples.english: I drank one gō of sake tonight.

examples.japanese: ⟦{家族|かぞく}→家族：00552_kazoku⟧{四人分|よにんぶん}なら{三合|さんごう}⟦{炊|た}けば→炊く：02127_taku⟧⟦{足|た}りる→足りる：01209_tariru⟧。
examples.english: Three gō of rice is enough for a family of four.

examples.japanese: ⟦{富士山|ふじさん}→富士山：09514_fujisan⟧⟦の→の：09472_no⟧{五合目|ごごうめ}⟦まで→まで：00490_made⟧⟦{車|くるま}→車：00516_kuruma⟧⟦で→で：00502_de⟧⟦{上|あ}がった→上がる：00615_agaru⟧。
examples.english: I drove up to the fifth station of Mt. Fuji.

examples.english: The mountain hut is between the seventh and eighth stations.

notes:
Part of the traditional Japanese measurement system ({尺貫法|しゃっかんほう}). One {合|ごう} ≈ 180 ml; one cup of uncooked rice is roughly one {合|ごう}, the standard amount measured by rice cookers.

VOLUME HIERARCHY:
- 1 {合|ごう} ≈ 180 ml
- 10 {合|ごう} = 1 ⟦{升|しょう}→升：26042_shou⟧ ≈ 1.8 L
- 10 ⟦{升|しょう}→升：26042_shou⟧ = 1 {斗|と} ≈ 18 L

COUNTING PATTERNS:
- {一合|いちごう}, {二合|にごう}, {三合|さんごう}, {四合|よんごう}, {五合|ごごう}

MOUNTAIN STATIONS:
The sense-2 usage with ⟦{目|め}→目：00525_me⟧ ({一合目|いちごうめ} etc.) divides mountain ascent into ten roughly equal sections. The {五合目|ごごうめ} of Mt. Fuji is the standard starting point for most modern climbers.

MODERN USE:
Sense 1 is still everyday vocabulary because rice is sold and cooked by the {合|ごう}, even though most other foods use metric measures. Sake is also commonly served by the {合|ごう} at traditional restaurants.
